name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVES_MATCH_Q01 - Wave propagation speeds across different physical media

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Transverse wave on a stretched stringI. \(\sqrt{\frac{Y}{\rho}}\)
B. Longitudinal wave in a fluid (bulk modulus \(B\))II. \(\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}\)
C. Longitudinal wave in an ideal gas (Laplace corrected)III. \(\sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}}\)
D. Longitudinal wave in a solid rod (Young's modulus \(Y\))IV. \(\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Wave speed on a stretched string
For a stretched string under tension \(T\) and having linear mass density \(\mu\), the restoring force is supplied by tension and the inertial parameter is \(\mu\). The transverse wave speed is given by \(v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}\). Thus, transverse wave on a stretched string corresponds to \(\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}\).

Step 2: Longitudinal wave speed in a fluid
In a fluid medium of bulk modulus \(B\) and mass density \(\rho\), compressions and rarefactions depend on the volume elasticity. The speed of a longitudinal wave is given by \(v = \sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}}\). Thus, longitudinal wave in a fluid corresponds to \(\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}}\).

Step 3: Laplace-corrected sound speed in an ideal gas
For an ideal gas, acoustic oscillations occur adiabatically with adiabatic bulk modulus \(B_{\text{ad}} = \gamma P\). The speed of sound is given by the Laplace formula \(v = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}}\). Thus, longitudinal wave in an ideal gas corresponds to \(\sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}}\).

Step 4: Longitudinal wave speed in a solid rod
In a slender solid bar or rod of Young's modulus \(Y\) and density \(\rho\), longitudinal strain dominates with negligible lateral restraint. The speed of longitudinal waves is given by \(v = \sqrt{\frac{Y}{\rho}}\). Thus, longitudinal wave in a solid rod corresponds to \(\sqrt{\frac{Y}{\rho}}\).

Step 5: Synthesis and Final Conclusion
Combining all four evaluated relationships yields the complete set of correspondences: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I.

Final Answer
A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVES_MATCH_Q02 - Physical quantities and fundamental wave relations

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Angular wave number (\(k\))I. \(|\nu_1 - \nu_2|\)
B. Angular frequency (\(\omega\))II. \(2a \cos\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)\)
C. Beat frequency (\(\nu_{\text{beat}}\))III. \(\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\)
D. Resultant amplitude in wave interference (\(A\))IV. \(\frac{2\pi}{T}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Angular wave number
The angular wave number (or propagation constant) represents the spatial frequency of the wave and is defined as \(k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\), where \(\lambda\) is the wavelength. Thus, angular wave number corresponds to \(\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\).

Step 2: Angular frequency
The angular frequency represents the temporal rate of change of phase and is related to the time period \(T\) by \(\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi \nu\). Thus, angular frequency corresponds to \(\frac{2\pi}{T}\).

Step 3: Beat frequency
When two harmonic sound waves of slightly different frequencies \(\nu_1\) and \(\nu_2\) interfere, the waxing and waning of acoustic intensity occurs at a frequency equal to the absolute difference \(\nu_{\text{beat}} = |\nu_1 - \nu_2|\). Thus, beat frequency corresponds to \(|\nu_1 - \nu_2|\).

Step 4: Resultant interference amplitude
When two identical sinusoidal waves of amplitude \(a\) interfere with a phase difference \(\phi\), trigonometric superposition yields a resultant wave amplitude of \(A = 2a \cos\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)\). Thus, resultant amplitude corresponds to \(2a \cos\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)\).

Step 5: Synthesis and Final Conclusion
Combining all four evaluated relationships yields the complete set of correspondences: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

Final Answer
A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVES_MATCH_Q03 - Boundary reflection characteristics and stationary wave nodes

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Reflection of a wave pulse from a rigid fixed boundaryI. Zero phase shift with maximum boundary displacement \(2a\)
B. Reflection of a wave pulse from an open free boundaryII. Phase reversal of \(\pi\) radians with zero boundary displacement
C. Position of nodes on a string fixed at both endsIII. \(\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{\lambda}{2}\) where \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\)
D. Position of antinodes on a string fixed at both endsIV. \(\frac{n\lambda}{2}\) where \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reflection at a rigid fixed boundary
At a rigid boundary, the string end is constrained to zero displacement (\(y = 0\)). The support exerts a reactive force producing an inverted reflected pulse. This produces a phase change of \(\pi\text{ radians}\) with permanent zero displacement at the boundary. Thus, reflection from a rigid fixed boundary corresponds to phase reversal of \(\pi\) radians with zero boundary displacement.

Step 2: Reflection at an open free boundary
At a completely free boundary, the end point is unrestricted and cannot support transverse force (\(\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = 0\)). The incident and reflected waves interfere constructively in phase (zero phase shift), creating a maximum displacement equal to twice the pulse amplitude (\(2a\)). Thus, reflection from an open free boundary corresponds to zero phase shift with maximum boundary displacement \(2a\).

Step 3: Positions of nodes on a fixed string
In the stationary wave \(y = 2a \sin(kx) \cos(\omega t)\) with boundary condition \(y(0) = 0\), nodes occur where \(\sin(kx) = 0\), yielding \(kx = n\pi\) or \(x = \frac{n\lambda}{2}\) for \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\). Thus, position of nodes corresponds to \(\frac{n\lambda}{2}\).

Step 4: Positions of antinodes on a fixed string
Antinodes occur where the amplitude \(|\sin(kx)| = 1\), yielding \(kx = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\pi\) or \(x = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{\lambda}{2}\) for \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\). Thus, position of antinodes corresponds to \(\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{\lambda}{2}\).

Step 5: Synthesis and Final Conclusion
Combining all four evaluated relationships yields the complete set of correspondences: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

Final Answer
A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVES_MATCH_Q04 - Resonant harmonic frequencies in strings and acoustic pipes

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I List-II
A. Fundamental mode of a string of length \(L\) fixed at both endsI. \(\frac{v}{L}\)
B. Fundamental mode of an organ pipe of length \(L\) closed at one endII. \(\frac{3v}{4L}\)
C. Second harmonic of an organ pipe of length \(L\) open at both endsIII. \(\frac{v}{2L}\)
D. Third harmonic of an organ pipe of length \(L\) closed at one endIV. \(\frac{v}{4L}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Fundamental mode of a string fixed at both ends
For a string of length \(L\) clamped at both ends, the fundamental mode corresponds to a single loop with \(L = \frac{\lambda}{2}\), giving wavelength \(\lambda = 2L\). The fundamental frequency is \(\nu_1 = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{v}{2L}\). Thus, fundamental mode of a string fixed at both ends corresponds to \(\frac{v}{2L}\).

Step 2: Fundamental mode of an organ pipe closed at one end
An organ pipe of length \(L\) closed at one end has a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. In the fundamental mode, \(L = \frac{\lambda}{4}\), giving \(\lambda = 4L\). The fundamental frequency is \(\nu_1 = \frac{v}{4L}\). Thus, fundamental mode of an organ pipe closed at one end corresponds to \(\frac{v}{4L}\).

Step 3: Second harmonic of an organ pipe open at both ends
An open organ pipe forms antinodes at both ends. Its harmonic frequencies are given by \(\nu_n = \frac{nv}{2L}\) for \(n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\). For the second harmonic (\(n = 2\)), the frequency is \(\nu_2 = 2\left(\frac{v}{2L}\right) = \frac{v}{L}\). Thus, second harmonic of an organ pipe open at both ends corresponds to \(\frac{v}{L}\).

Step 4: Third harmonic of an organ pipe closed at one end
An organ pipe closed at one end produces only odd harmonics, given by \(\nu_n = (2n - 1)\frac{v}{4L}\). The fundamental mode (\(n = 1\)) is \(\frac{v}{4L}\), and the next higher mode is the third harmonic, which is three times the fundamental frequency: \(\nu_3 = 3\left(\frac{v}{4L}\right) = \frac{3v}{4L}\). Thus, third harmonic of an organ pipe closed at one end corresponds to \(\frac{3v}{4L}\).

Step 5: Synthesis and Final Conclusion
Combining all four evaluated relationships yields the complete set of correspondences: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

Final Answer
A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
